clinicalPearls: Coccidian protozoan acquired by ingesting mature oocysts from faecally contaminated food or water, chiefly in tropical and subtropical regions
Causes watery, non-bloody diarrhoea with cramping, weight loss and low-grade fever, which can become chronic and severe in people with advanced HIV or other immunosuppression
Peripheral eosinophilia is characteristic and helps distinguish it from most other enteric protozoa, which do not raise the eosinophil count
Large elliptical oocysts are shed intermittently and are best detected using a modified acid-fast (Kinyoun) stain, appearing as pink-red structures on the smear
Oocysts also autofluoresce under ultraviolet microscopy, providing a rapid screening adjunct in laboratories with the facility
Cotrimoxazole is the treatment of choice, with prolonged or suppressive courses often required in immunocompromised hosts to prevent relapse
Restoring immune function with antiretroviral therapy is central to durable cure in HIV-associated disease
reference.pathophysiology: Cystoisospora belli is an obligate intracellular coccidian parasite of the small-intestinal epithelium. Sporulated oocysts ingested from contaminated food or water release sporozoites that invade enterocytes, where the parasite undergoes both asexual and sexual replication before immature oocysts are passed in the stool and mature in the environment. Epithelial invasion produces villous blunting, crypt hyperplasia and a mucosal inflammatory infiltrate rich in eosinophils, impairing absorption and driving a secretory, watery diarrhoea. In immunocompetent people the illness is usually self-limiting, but defective cell-mediated immunity permits heavy, persistent infection, extraintestinal spread and chronic malabsorption.
additionalInvestigations: Stool microscopy for ova, cysts and parasites with modified acid-fast staining
Ultraviolet autofluorescence microscopy of faecal smears
Repeated stool sampling because oocyst shedding is intermittent
Full blood count looking for peripheral eosinophilia
HIV testing and CD4 count in prolonged or severe disease
Small-bowel biopsy when stool examination is repeatedly negative
redFlags: Profuse dehydrating diarrhoea with hypovolaemia and electrolyte disturbance
Chronic diarrhoea with progressive weight loss suggesting underlying immunosuppression
Extraintestinal or disseminated disease in advanced HIV
Failure to respond to first-line therapy raising the possibility of relapse or coinfection
reference.prognosis: Immunocompetent patients usually recover fully, though relapses can occur; in immunocompromised hosts the illness may be chronic and debilitating, but responds well to antimicrobial therapy combined with immune reconstitution.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis because routine stool microscopy without acid-fast staining fails to reveal the oocysts
Interpreting a single negative stool as excluding infection despite intermittent shedding
Overlooking the clue of eosinophilia, which is unusual among enteric protozoa
Stopping treatment too early in immunosuppressed patients, allowing relapse
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Treat with cotrimoxazole as the antimicrobial of choice to clear the coccidian infection and resolve the diarrhoea
Use ciprofloxacin or pyrimethamine with folinic acid as alternatives in patients intolerant of sulphonamides
Give prolonged courses and secondary prophylaxis in immunocompromised hosts, in whom relapse is frequent
Optimise antiretroviral therapy to achieve immune reconstitution in HIV-associated disease
Provide supportive rehydration, electrolyte correction and nutritional support during chronic or severe illness
Advise food and water hygiene to prevent reinfection, and test for HIV with CD4 count in prolonged or severe disease
